section_title: Meaning and limits of clinical equivalence
text: Two target contours should be considered clinically equivalent when their expected outcomes differ by less than a prespecified, clinically justified tolerance for each relevant tumour control and toxicity endpoint, for the same patient and treatment context.

section_title: Meaning and limits of clinical equivalence
text: Expert agreement that two target contours are clinically acceptable is sufficient to classify them as clinically equivalent.

section_title: Meaning and limits of clinical equivalence
text: A target contour that does not conform to clinical guidelines (e.g. is not technically protocol compliant) should be corrected, even if its predicted outcome difference is within the agreed tolerance.

section_title: Meaning and limits of clinical equivalence
text: When for a given patient multiple contours are available that have been judged to be clinically equivalent, the smallest should be preferred for treatment planning

section_title: Meaning and limits of clinical equivalence
text: Where functional imaging contributes to defining the target volume, that information should also inform the definition of its equivalence range.
Before defining an acceptable contour range, a contouring guideline or documented clinical agreement should specify what the target is intended to include.
Inner and outer contours drawn by experts on representative cases are a reasonable proxy for constructing a candidate clinically equivalent range.
The intersection (inner boundary) and union (outer boundary) of protocol-compliant expert target contours are sufficient to define a clinically acceptable range.
When tumour-control modelling is used to assess equivalence ranges, its predictions should be evaluated alongside available recurrence-pattern data relevant to the tumour site and target type.
Models of disease spread and treatment outcome (such as TCP/NTCP) are a reasonable basis for constructing candidate ranges, provided their uncertainty is accounted for.

Before a contour range is described as clinically equivalent, its use should be supported by prospective patient outcome data demonstrating equivalence within prespecified tolerances. (i.e. Surrogates such as expert consensus, model prediction, or dose equivalence are not sufficient)
Acceptable ranges need to be constructed on a patient specific basis.
Using dose equivalence is a reasonable basis for identifying candidate limits of equivalent contour variation when reliable outcome models are unavailable.

Validation of the contour range should be done by including plans optimised using different contours within the candidate range, with all plans assessed against the same independently specified evaluation target.

Equivalence bands will always be constructed based on stochastic components. Therefore, equivalence bands will only be valid for an average patient or proportion of patients, it may not be applicable to the whole population.
